list.listitem: Consistent screening is recommended in the neonatal period, at 6 months, and at 3 years. C
Amblyopia is a clinical diagnosis; if suspected, the patient should be referred for confirmation of the diagnosis by an ophthalmologist. C
After addressing amblyogenic risk factors, penalizing the sound eye with patching or cycloplegics is the mainstay of therapy to preserve binocular vision. A

background.definition: Amblyopia is typically a unilateral (rarely bilateral) reduction of the best corrected visual acuity, caused by conditions that affect normal visual development.

list.listitem: In North America, 20 to 40 affected per 1000 people.
Occurs in about 1 to 4 percent of children.
Causes more cases of childhood onset unilateral visual reduction or loss than all other potential causes combined.
Impaired depth perception is the most common deficit associated with amblyopia, which may have a significant impact on future visuomotor tasks (playing sports, walking, driving).

Strabismus: This is the most common cause of amblyopia. A child's deviated eye prevents binocular participation in visual activities. Visual input through the misaligned eye is ignored, leading to abnormal development of visual pathways for the affected eye. It is possible, however, for visual fixation to freely alternate between eyes, in which case amblyopia is less likely to develop. Although vertical deviations rarely occur, pediatric strabismus usually involves an eye temporally deviated (exotropia), or more commonly, nasally deviated (esotropia). Risk factors for strabismus include low birth weight, retinopathy of prematurity, smoking during pregnancy, anisometropia, hyperopia, and inheritance.

Anisometropia: The second most common cause of amblyopia. Refractive power required to provide the clearest image in each eye differs to such a degree that no meaningful visual stimuli are detected in the affected eye. This results in insufficient development of the visual pathways. Rarely, high refractive errors in both eyes may go undetected, resulting in bilateral amblyopia.

Visual deprivation: This is the least common cause of amblyopia but most difficult to treat. Deprivation may result from some form of congenital or infantile ocular pathology (ie, blepharoptosis, congenital cataracts, corneal opacities, vitreous hemorrhage, or ocular tumors) that restricts visual input during the critical period of visual pathway development.
Esotropia ("crossed eyes"): inward deviation of the eye(s). Causes include genetic syndromes including Down syndrome, brain abnormalities, severe hyperopia, and a history of amblopia or strabismus.

Development of visual pathways begins around the eighth week of gestation and continues through approximately the age of 7 years. Upon birth, visual stimuli guide development of appropriate neuronal pathways.

A crucial part of this process occurs during the period of nerve fiber myelination, which continues from birth to about 2 years of age. Maturation continues to about 7 years of age when a reduction in plasticity of the visual pathways can be observed.
Any disruption or imbalance in stimulation of the visual system during development can result in permanent inability to perceive images clearly.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Family history (first degree relative with amblyopia)

list.listitem: Newborn's eyes should be examined for general eye health, including a red reflex test in the nursery and during initial outpatient newborn exams. C
The United States Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) recommends vision screening for all children at least once between the ages of 3 and 5 years, although randomized trial data are lacking. B
Ophthalmologists should examine all high-risk infants regularly up to age 5. C
Preterm infants should be screened for retinopathy of prematurity (ROP).

A primary care provider should examine a newborn's eyes for general eye health, including a red reflex test in the nursery. However, randomized controlled trials regarding screening have not been performed. An RCT of a more intensive protocol of screening compared to a standard protocol has proved to have possible benefit, although it is resource intensive. A smartphone app, GoCheck kids, was useful in detecting amblyopia risk factors in young children 6 months to 6 years old who were uncooperative, with the with a PPV 57% and NPV 83%.

An ophthalmologist should be asked to examine all infants at high risk of ROP, those with a family history of retinoblastoma, glaucoma, or cataracts in childhood, retinal dystrophy/degeneration or systemic diseases associated with eye problems, or when any opacity of the ocular media or nystagmus (purposeless rhythmic movement of the eyes) is seen. Infants with neurodevelopmental delay should also be examined by an ophthalmologist.

By 6 months to 1 year of age, all infants should be screened for ocular health, including a red reflex test by a properly trained health care provider such as an ophthalmologist, pediatrician, family physician, nurse, or physician assistant during routine well-baby follow-up visits.

Vision screening should also be performed between the ages of 3 and 3 1/2 years. Vision and alignment should be assessed by a pediatrician, family practitioner, ophthalmologist, optometrist, orthoptist, or an individual trained in vision assessment of preschool children. Emphasis should be placed on checking visual acuity as soon as a child is cooperative enough to complete the examination. Generally, this occurs between the ages of 2 1/2 and 3 1/2 years. It is essential that a formal testing of visual acuity be performed by the age of 5 years. The USPSTF recommendation is to screen at some point between the ages of 3 and 5 years.

Further screening examinations should be done at routine school checks or after the appearance of symptoms. Routine comprehensive professional eye examination of the normal asymptomatic child has no proven medical benefit.
Amblyopia in childhood is a clinical diagnosis, with an abnormal or asymmetric red reflex, abnormal occluded visual fixation, or abnormal visual acuity testing. C
History should include past medical and family histories of strabismus, refractive errors, and organic eye disease in the child. C
Strabismus may either be primary or secondary, and it is best detected with evaluation of the corneal light reflex along with cover testing. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Broad nasal bridge with prominent epicanthal folds, red reflex equal, pupillary reflex central

list.listitem: The history should address premature birth, congenital or neonatal infections, family history of eye disease, including high refractive errors and strabismus, and previous eye trauma. Caregivers of the patient may report intermittent ocular misaligment.

Fully appreciating a child's visual ability is challenging for most generalists involved in screening exams. Clues to abnormal vision in an infant include nystagmus, inattention to colorful targets either at distance or near, objection to occlusion of one eye, or observed ocular misalignment. Children older than 3 years may be able to participate in acuity testing; such testing should be done with each eye individually.
The Bruckner test involves using a direct ophthalmoscope to illicit the red reflex of both eyes simultaneously. Any asymmetry is abnormal and warrants referral to an ophthalmologist.

The Hirschberg test assists in detecting strabismus using a centrally held focal light source to illicit the corneal light reflex. While fixating on the examiner's light, the light reflex should be seen in the center of the patient's pupil. Any asymmetry of this reflex is abnormal and warrants referral to an ophthalmologist. Cover-uncover and alternate cover testing augment the examiner's ability to detect and measure strabismus.
The purpose of any and all primary care diagnostic tools is to identify those children who are at risk for, or are suspected to have, amblyopia or stabismus.
Any such suspicion warrants referral to an ophthalmologist for more sensitive and specific evaluation.
Treatment of refractive error alone is the initial step in care of children 0––17 years of age with amblyopia.

Patching or penalizing the preferentially fixating eye is initiated for children who do not improve with eye glasses alone, either with physical occlusion or administration of topical cycloplegic agents.
A
Treat amblyogenic risk factors. B

Pharmacologic penalization of the better eye with atropine 1% or homatropine 5% ophthalmic solutions is frequently used. Cycloplegia (loss of accommodative power) occurs as a result, and the patient is forced to use the amblyopic eye, often resulting in improved vision. All treatments are generally most effective in children under the age of 7 years and should be monitored closely by an ophthalmologist.
Recent studies suggest that occlusive patching (see below) may provide a better vision improvement over a shorter period of time, but pharmacologic penalization is easier to use and often cheaper.
A Cochrane systematic review identified three studies with 525 amblyopic eyes. They found that both atropine penalization and occlusion are similarly effective.

A study randomized 108 children (mean age 5.2 years) with severe amblyopia to combined atropine and patching therapy or patching alone. The improvement in visual acuity was significantly greater at 6 months in the combined therapy group by 1.4 lines. However, it is not clear whether this is a clinically important difference.
Appropriate surgical correction of strabismus or organic causes of visual deprivation are essential to amblyopia prevention and treatment.

Botulinum toxin injection has been studied in 6 RCTs identified by a Cochrane review, which found no benefit or a slightly reduced chance of recovering correct alignment of the eyes compared with surgery.

For patients with esotropia, a Cochrane review identified 2 RCTs with 234 children. The first compared 3 botulinum toxin injections with surgery (bimedial rectus muscle recession) and found some evidence of better outcomes with surgery. The second study compared unilateral with bilateral surgery and found no important differences between groups.
A systematic review found no studies comparing adjustable with nonadjustable sutures.

Full- or part-time physical occlusion of the better eye during periods of peak activity as directed by an ophthalmologist is the traditional recommended therapy. A randomized trial found that 6 hours of patching was as good as full-time patching for children with severe amblyopia.

Children with moderate to severe ambylopia derive the greatest benefit from treatment. One study of 177 children between the ages of 3 and 5 years randomized to no treatment, corrective glasses, or corrective glasses with patching; the researchers found no difference in visual acuity at 1.5 years in the children with only mild amblyopia at the beginning of the study.
A Cochrane review found no randomized controlled trials of occlusion for stimulus deprivation amblyopia.
Adhesive patches are often used but can be poorly tolerated; compliance is more difficult to enforce for both parents and doctors. Pharmocologic penalization may be necessary, as described above.
Correct any significant refractive errors with corrective lenses as directed by an ophthalmologist.

A randomized trial of children with amblyopia and mild visual impairment found that eyeglasses plus patching was not significantly better than eyeglasses alone, but children with moderate or worse impairment do benefit.
Specific interventions for stimulus deprivation amblyopia have not been studied.

Intermittent occlusion therapy using liquid crystal eyeglasses has been introduced as an alternative treatment for amblyopia that may be associated with better treatment compliance. The eyeglasses alternate between a clear and opaque lens in the stronger eye, using an electronic shutter.
Clinical responses can occur as early as 1 week or persist despite treatment of underlying conditions.

Primary treatment should be abandoned if no progress is demonstrated over 3 to 6 months with good compliance. Additional testing or adjunct therapies may be required to re-evaluate for other etiologies of visual loss.

A study by the Pediatric Eye Disease Investigator Group of treatment of moderate strabismic and/or anisometropic amblyopia demonstrated that the visual acuity of the amblyopic eye improved to 20/30 or better 6 months after initiating treatment in approximately three–quarters of children under 7 years of age.
Referral to an ophthalmologist is necessary in all cases of suspected amblyopia or related eye disease.
Untreated disease in the developing eye can lead to profound and irreversible vision loss. C
Patients with a large esotropia are unlikely to spontaneously resolve. B

Significant vision improvement is often obtained with treatment. On average, visual acuity is roughly 2 lines worse than the sound eye. The most important prognostic factor is visual acuity at time of diagnosis. C

Careful follow-up by an ophthalmologist, particularly in children undergoing occlusive or pharmacologic penalization, is required for monitoring of improvement and prevention of reverse amblyopia of the sound eye. C
Education of parents is essential to stress importance of follow-up in the care of their child to prevent permanent vision loss. C
Although some adults are not diagnosed with amblyopia until later in life due to insufficient screening, the development of amblyopia is a pediatric process.
New onset strabismus or detection of significant vision loss in one or both eyes of an adult warrants referral to or consultation with an ophthalmologist for further evaluation.
